title: McGuffey's Third Eclectic Reader
sourceTitle: McGuffey's Third Eclectic Reader, Revised Edition
author: William Holmes McGuffey
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #14766: 'Public domain in the USA.' Revised edition first copyrighted 1879 (Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co.); renewals 1896 (American Book Company) and 1907 and 1920 (H. H. Vail), all before 1930.
description: The classic Third Reader: 79 stories, fables, poems, and nature lessons, from the boy who cried wolf and the clever way to weigh an elephant to beavers, bats, hummingbirds, and Wordsworth's “We Are Seven.” Each day your child learns a few new words, reads the lesson aloud, and narrates it back or learns a few lines of a poem by heart. The full text is free online.
includes: 80 lessons in 10 units: the introduction plus all 79 Third Reader lessons
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Key new words, a reading activity, and narration, copywork, or memory work each day
Poem authors, dated content, and the two untranscribed script lessons flagged in the notes

lessons.title: Getting Started: Sounds, Emphasis, and Punctuation
steps: Say the long and short vowel sounds from the tables together, then a few subvocals and aspirates
Read the emphasis questions aloud, stressing the word that answers each one (“Did you ride to town? No, I walked.”)
Find a hyphen, comma, dash, quotation marks, and an apostrophe on the Punctuation page and say what each one does
questions: What is emphasis?
What does an apostrophe show?
answers: Saying some words with more force than others because the meaning depends on them
That letters are left out (o'er, 't is), or who owns something (Helen's book)
lessons.notes: The book's introductory pages. Return to the sound tables for a minute or two of drill before lessons all year.

lessons.title: Lesson I: The Shepherd Boy
steps: New words: pasture, brooklet, crook, glossy, horse-chestnuts, jackstones
Read the poem aloud to your child, then take turns reading a stanza each
Narrate: what were Roy's 'sheep,' 'cows,' and 'pasture' really made of?
Copywork: “And the sparkle was all in his eyes.”
questions: Where was Roy really playing?
What were Roy's sheep?
What did big brother Walter do while Roy slept?
answers: Indoors, at a table in a house in town, on a rainy day
Snowy-white pebbles from the seashore
Cut the cows (horse-chestnuts) into baskets and turned the sheep (pebbles) into jackstones
lessons.notes: Poem by Emily S. Oakey. Jackstones is an old name for jacks. Let your child set up a pretend farm from things in the house afterward.

lessons.title: Lesson II: Johnny's First Snowstorm
steps: New words: snowstorm, orange groves, joyfully, feathery, several
Let your child read the lesson aloud; you read Johnny's mother's lines
Narrate: what did Johnny think the snow was before his mother explained?
If it's snowing, catch a flake on dark cloth and look with a magnifying glass
questions: Why had Johnny never seen snow?
What did the snowflake look like under the glass?
Which did Johnny decide he liked better, snowballs or oranges?
answers: He had lived in a warm country
A pretty little star
Snowballs

lessons.title: Lesson III: Let It Rain
steps: New words: quench, thirst, shocking, wreaths, ground (as in a mill)
Read it as a play: you are Father, your child is Rose
Narrate: list all the good things the rain does that Father helped Rose see
Copywork: “I am truly very glad to see the rain falling.”
questions: Why was Rose unhappy at the start?
How does rain help make bread?
answers: It was raining and she had to stay indoors
It makes the wheat grow, and water turns the mill that grinds the wheat into flour
lessons.notes: A dialogue: point out how the speaker's name comes before each speech.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: Castle-Building
steps: New words: dismay, mimic, fiercely, passion, foundation
Read the lesson aloud together, a paragraph each
Narrate: what happened to Herbert's castle, and what did he do next?
questions: What knocked down Herbert's castle?
Who protected the cat?
What did Papa do to help?
answers: The cat rubbed against it
His little sister Hetty
Sat on the floor and began building a new castle with him
lessons.notes: Part 1 of 2; the story finishes in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson V: Castle-Building (Concluded)
steps: New words: retorted, heedlessly, guard, forehead
Let your child read the lesson aloud; help with the conversation parts
Narrate: what does 'crying over spilled milk' mean, and how did Papa say to handle trouble?
Copywork: “If your castles get knocked down, build them up again.”
questions: What had made Joe cry once?
What should Herbert do if the cat knocks the castle down again?
answers: His kite string broke and he lost his kite
Build it up again

lessons.title: Lesson VI: Lend a Hand
steps: Look at the Lesson VI heading in the online text; the script page itself is not included
If you have a print or scanned copy, read the script poem together and copy two lines
Otherwise, talk about one way your child can 'lend a hand' at home today and do it
questions: What does it mean to 'lend a hand'?
answers: To help someone
lessons.notes: Script lesson: the Gutenberg edition has only the title (the cursive page is not transcribed). Use a print copy or treat this as a short helping-day lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson VII: The Truant
steps: New words: truant, falsely, haste, ignorant, conduct
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you
Narrate: tell what happened to James on the day he went to the boats
questions: What does it mean to 'play truant'?
Where did James get his money?
Who saved the boys?
answers: To stay away from school without permission
From his aunt
Some men who rowed out to them in a boat

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: The White Kitten
steps: New words: frolic, counsel, needful, beggar-like
Read the poem aloud with expression; let your child read it back
Memorize: the last two lines, “It is needful that they / Should this counsel obey, / And be careful in choosing their places to play.”
questions: How did the kitten look when she came home at night?
What lesson does the poem give children?
answers: Dirty, with gray streaks and a black nose
Be careful where you choose to play (and keep yourself good)
lessons.notes: Poem: read it twice, the second time with feeling.

lessons.title: Lesson IX: The Beaver
steps: New words: chiefly, material, commence, gnawing, trappers, inhuman
Your child reads the lesson aloud; stop after each paragraph to picture it
Narrate: how does a beaver build its dam and hut?
Look at a picture of a beaver lodge online or in a book
questions: Why do beavers build near water?
What do beavers eat in winter?
Why didn't the gentleman shoot the young beavers?
answers: They swim more easily than they walk
The bark they peel and store
Their play reminded him of children he knew, and it seemed cruel
lessons.notes: Fur trapping was ordinary in 1879; talk about how we protect wild animals today.

lessons.title: Lesson X: The Young Teacher
steps: New words: amuse, inquire, venture, confused, parcels, copybook
Read the lesson together, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: how did Charles use his free hour, and what did his father find?
questions: Why couldn't Joe go to school?
What did Charles's father think he was doing at first?
What did Charles's father give the boys?
answers: His parents were too poor
Going out on the river in the fisherman's boat
Books, writing paper, pens, and ink
lessons.notes: Joe's mother 'kept her wheel going': she spun thread on a spinning wheel to earn money.

lessons.title: Lesson XI: The Blacksmith
steps: New words: forge, aweary, shrink, intense
Read the poem aloud, tapping a 'hammer' on the table for each “Clink, clink”
Memorize: the first stanza
Copywork: “We'll work each form / While the iron is warm”
questions: Why is a blacksmith's face black?
What does the blacksmith make with many links?
answers: From the soot and smoke of the forge fire
A chain
lessons.notes: Poem. 'Strike while the iron is hot' comes from blacksmith work: talk about what it means.

lessons.title: Lesson XII: A Walk in the Garden
steps: New words: gravel, meddle, borders, admiring, rare
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only with hard words
Narrate: compare Frank with the boy at the gate
questions: What did Frank's mother ask him to promise?
Why wouldn't the gardener let the other boy in?
What did the gardener give Frank and his mother?
answers: Not to meddle with anything in the garden
He had meddled with the flowers and picked rare fruit the day before
Some pretty flowers

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: The Wolf
steps: New words: forest, village, earnest, dismay, deceived
Read the lesson aloud together
Narrate: tell the story of the boy who cried wolf in your own words
Copywork: “The truth itself is not believed, / From one who often has deceived.”
questions: Why did John cry 'Wolf!' the first time?
What happened when the wolf really came?
answers: To have some fun
No one came to help, and the wolf killed many sheep, including John's lamb
lessons.notes: This is the old fable of the boy who cried wolf.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: The Little Bird's Song
steps: New words: melody, modest, unnoticed, Maker
Read the poem aloud; let your child read Gracie's words and you read Father's
Memorize: the last stanza, “So live, my child, all through your life …”
questions: Why couldn't the people see the bird?
What lesson did Father want Gracie to learn?
answers: It was small and plain brown, so it didn't show
To do good without trying to be seen or praised
lessons.notes: Poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XV: Harry and Annie
steps: New words: exploring, pretend, thaw, good-naturedly, disobedient
Read the lesson aloud, a paragraph each
Narrate: what did Harry say to excuse himself, and was he right?
questions: What did mother ask the children not to do?
Who saved Annie?
What did Harry do when he got home?
answers: Not to cross the pond, because the ice was thawing
A man working near the shore
Told his mother how disobedient he had been
lessons.notes: A good time to go over ice safety rules for your family.

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: Bird Friends
steps: New words: grove, rod (a measure), faith, crumbs, bedpost
Read it aloud to your child, then let them read their favorite part back
Narrate: how did the old man win the birds' trust?
Put out crumbs or seed and watch who comes
questions: Why did the birds follow the old man's rake?
How did the birds wake him in the morning?
What made the birds trust him?
answers: To catch the worms in the fresh dirt
They sat on his bedpost and chirped
His kind eyes and voice
lessons.notes: Adapted from Elihu Burritt. A rod is about 16½ feet.

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: What the Minutes Say
steps: New words: furnished, unseen, track
Read the short poem aloud twice
Memorize: the whole poem (eight lines)
Set a one-minute timer and see how much you can tidy in it
questions: How many 'wings' does each minute have?
What happens to someone who loses minutes?
answers: Sixty (seconds)
They lose whole years
lessons.notes: Poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: The Widow and the Merchant
steps: New words: merchant, widow, assistance, hesitation, convinced, check
Let your child read the lesson aloud; you read the banker's lines
Narrate: tell what happened at the bank, step by step
questions: How much did the widow ask for?
Why did the widow go back instead of keeping the money?
How much did she get in the end?
answers: Five dollars
She was honest and thought it was a mistake
Five hundred dollars
lessons.notes: Dollar amounts are from 1879; five dollars was then several days' wages.

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: The Birds Set Free
steps: New words: prisoners, apiece, bargain, resolved
Read the lesson together
Narrate: why did the man let the birds go?
questions: How much did each bird cost?
How much did the man pay for them all?
Where had the man been a prisoner?
answers: Fifty cents
Five dollars
In a French prison, as a prisoner of war

lessons.title: Lesson XX: A Moment Too Late
steps: New words: downy, disturbed, petals, sped
Read the poem aloud; your child reads stanzas 5 and 6
Copywork: “Better be an hour early, and stand and wait”
questions: What happened to the bird's nest?
What did the bee miss?
answers: The wind blew it away
The honey had already dropped from the flower
lessons.notes: Poem. 'Staid' is an old spelling of 'stayed.'

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: Humming Birds
steps: New words: crest, brilliant, adorn, fibers, instinct, approach
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: describe the hummingbird's nest and eggs
Watch a short slow-motion video of hummingbird wings
questions: Why are they called humming birds?
How big were the eggs?
How does the mother bird protect her nest?
answers: Their fast-moving wings make a humming sound
About as large as a small sugarplum
She darts at you and pecks at your eyes

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: The Wind and the Sun
steps: New words: dispute, blast, mantle, sultry, forcibly, fable
Read the fable aloud, then act it out with a blanket as the cloak
Narrate: tell the fable in three sentences
questions: What contest did the Wind and the Sun agree on?
Who won?
What is the lesson?
answers: To see who could make a traveler take off his cloak
The Sun
Gentleness often succeeds where force fails
lessons.notes: An Aesop fable.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: Sunset
steps: Look at the Lesson XXIII heading in the online text; the script page is not transcribed
If you have a print copy, read the script lines and copy one
Otherwise, watch tonight's sunset together and name its colors
questions: What colors do you see in a sunset?
lessons.notes: Script lesson: the Gutenberg edition has only the title. Use a print copy, or make it a sunset-watching day.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: Beautiful Hands
steps: New words: coarse, opinion, deeds, cheerfully, ashamed
Read it as a conversation: you are Miss Roberts, your child is Daisy
Narrate: list the things Mary's hands do
Copywork: “The good alone are really beautiful.”
questions: Why did Daisy think Mary's hands were ugly?
Why did Miss Roberts call them beautiful?
answers: They were red and hard
They are always busy doing kind, helpful work, and do it gladly

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: Things to Remember
steps: New words: protection, peevish, pout, manners, secret
Read the lesson aloud, one numbered rule each
Narrate: choose three rules and say them in your own words
Pick one rule to practice all week
questions: How should you ask for food at the table?
What should you think about at night before sleep?
answers: Ask someone to pass it instead of reaching
Whether you did anything wrong that day, ask forgiveness, and forgive others
lessons.notes: A list of manners and devotional rules; trim or discuss to suit your family.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: Three Little Mice
steps: New words: cunning, lattice, protruded, perplexed, comical
Read the poem aloud for your child; then let them read a stanza
Narrate: what happened when the narrator caught a mouse's tail?
questions: What color were the mice?
How did the mice ask for food?
What did the other mice do to 'help'?
answers: White, with red eyes
They stood up in a row, folding their paws and rattling the bars
Began to gnaw off the tail
lessons.notes: Poem by Julia C. R. Dorr. Long lines: read slowly.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: The New Year
steps: New words: gayly, distress, gratitude, doubtless, wretched
Let your child read the lesson aloud
Narrate: what did Edward plan to do with his money, and what did he do instead?
questions: What did Edward's father give him?
Why couldn't the man answer Edward?
What reward did Edward get?
answers: Two silver dollars
He spoke only German, not English
A whole bundle of books

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: The Clock and the Sundial
steps: New words: steeple, stock (a post), boasting, folly, modesty, moral
Read the fable aloud, giving the clock a proud voice
Narrate: why was the clock wrong to boast?
questions: Why did the clock call the sundial stupid?
What did the sun show when it came out?
answers: The sundial can only tell time when the sun shines
That the clock was half an hour behind
lessons.notes: Make a simple sundial with a stick in the yard on a sunny day.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: Remember
steps: New words: ever-wakeful, falsehood, forgiveness, delight
Read the poem aloud together, slowly
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: Who does the poem say sees all we do?
What should you do if you have done wrong?
answers: God
Be sorry and pray to be forgiven
lessons.notes: A devotional poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: Courage and Cowardice
steps: New words: quarrel, mischief, reproach, deserved, schoolmates
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns
Narrate: who really showed courage, and how?
Copywork: “Never be afraid to do good, but always fear to do evil.”
questions: Why wouldn't Henry go see the fight?
What happened to Robert while bathing?
answers: He did not want to meddle or get into trouble
He went out of his depth and Henry saved him from drowning
lessons.notes: Today we teach children to call an adult or throw something that floats rather than swim out to rescue someone.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Weighing an Elephant
steps: New words: gratitude, deliverance, vowed, enormous, expense
Read the lesson aloud; stop at paragraph 8 and let your child guess the answer first
Narrate: explain the sailor's trick step by step
Try it: float a bowl in water, mark the waterline with a toy in it, then match the mark with coins
questions: What did the king promise to give the poor?
Where did Teddy put the elephant?
What did Teddy win?
answers: The elephant's weight in silver
In a boat
An orange
lessons.notes: Adapted from A. L. O. E.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: The Soldier
steps: New words: arrayed, contest, warrior, enlist, mustered
Read the poem aloud with a marching beat
Narrate: what kind of soldier does the speaker want to be?
questions: Does the soldier in the poem want to shed blood?
What does he fight for?
answers: No
Truth (and love)
lessons.notes: Poem by J. G. Adams.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: The Echo
steps: New words: rambling, mocking, thicket, offended, peevish
Read the lesson together; you read Mother's part
Narrate: what is an echo, and what did Robert's mother teach with it?
Copywork: “A soft answer turneth away wrath.”
questions: Who did Robert think was mocking him?
How did his mother explain an echo?
answers: A boy hiding in the woods
Like a ball bouncing back off a wall, your voice comes back from a hill

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: George's Feast
steps: New words: blazing, collect, scarlet, refresh, longing
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell how George decided what to do with the strawberries
questions: Why did George go to the woods?
Who were the strawberries for in the end?
answers: To gather sticks for the fire
His sick mother

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: The Lord's Prayer
steps: New words: hallow, bounty, transgressions, compassion, temptation
Read the verse version aloud, then compare it with Matthew 6:9–13
Memorize: the first stanza (or the prayer in your family's version)
questions: What does 'our portion of bread' ask for?
What does the poem ask God to keep us from?
answers: Food for each day
Temptation, weakness, and sin
lessons.notes: A verse paraphrase. The script page that follows (An Evening Prayer) is not transcribed in the Gutenberg text; use a print copy if you have one.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: Finding the Owner
steps: New words: evident, satisfaction, critical, conscious, anxiety
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns
Narrate: why didn't Fred enjoy the knife at first?
questions: Whose knife was it?
How did Fred feel while he kept it?
What did the doctor do?
answers: Dr. Perry's
Like a thief; worried all week
Let Fred keep it

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII: Bats
steps: New words: crevices, quadruped, prowling, devour, policy
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: how did the bat trick the owl and then the cat?
questions: What are a bat's wings made of?
What did the bat tell the owl?
What did the bat tell the cat?
answers: Thin skin stretched over bones
That he was not a bird but like a mouse
That he was a bird, not a mouse
lessons.notes: Adapted from S. G. Goodrich. Bats are mammals; the fable's harsh ending is about being two-faced, not about real bats, which are helpful insect-eaters.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII: A Summer Day
steps: New words: tints, sheaves, lance, lowing
Read the poem aloud, one stanza each
Copywork: “This is the way the morning dawns”
Draw one stanza's picture
questions: What are the cows doing at evening?
What do fireflies do in the poem?
answers: Lowing (mooing) in the lane
Wink on hill and plain
lessons.notes: Poem by George Cooper.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: I Will Think of It
steps: New words: chandelier, pendulum, mainspring, whalebone, lectures, motto
Your child reads the lesson aloud; pause after each inventor
Narrate: name the four thinkers and what set each one thinking
questions: What did Newton see fall?
What did James Watt watch move?
What was James Ferguson's motto?
answers: An apple
The lid of a teakettle, pushed by steam
“I will think of it”
lessons.notes: The Newton apple story is a well-loved legend. Find Pisa and Scotland on a map.

lessons.title: Lesson XL: Charlie and Rob
steps: New words: hinder, kindling, conquer, splendid, accounts, chores
Read it as a dialogue: you are Charlie, your child is Rob
Narrate: how are Charlie's and Rob's ideas about work different?
questions: How does Rob make splitting wood fun?
How is Rob 'working toward' being a bank clerk?
Which boy do you think did well, and why?
answers: He pretends the tough stick is a hard lesson to conquer
By keeping his father's account books
Rob, who worked steadily and honestly; the story hints that Charlie ended up a tramp
lessons.notes: The ending asks a question; let your child answer it. 'Tramps' meant homeless wanderers.

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: Ray and His Kite
steps: New words: companions, daydreams, lantern, comet, hobgoblin, approached
Read the lesson aloud together, a paragraph each
Narrate: what did the villagers guess the light was?
questions: What did Ray tie to his kite?
Where was Ray while the men looked at the light?
What did the men decide to do?
answers: A tin lantern
Sitting in a fence corner behind a tree
Keep the secret and enjoy the joke
lessons.notes: Never fly a kite with a flame or near power lines; this one is just a story.

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: Beware of the First Drink
steps: New words: ramble, decent, debts, resist, sot
Read the lesson aloud with your child
Narrate: tell how Tom Smith's life went wrong, step by step
questions: What kind of boy was Tom Smith at school?
What did Tom himself say to beware of?
Where was Tom sent at the end?
answers: Decent and well-behaved
The first drink
To state prison for ten years
lessons.notes: A temperance lesson, common in 1870s readers. Preview it and discuss in a way that fits your family.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: Speak Gently
steps: New words: mar, accents, aged, careworn, erring, eternity
Read the poem aloud softly, as the title says
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: Name two kinds of people the poem says to speak gently to.
Why is it better to rule by love than by fear?
answers: Any two: little children, the aged, the poor, those who do wrong
Kind words win love and do lasting good; harsh words spoil it
lessons.notes: Poem by George Washington Langford.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: The Seven Sticks
steps: New words: quarreling, property, strained, vain, union, prosper
Read the lesson aloud
Try it: tie several pencils or sticks together and try to bend them, then one alone
Copywork: “Home, city, country, all are prosperous found, / When by the powerful link of union bound.”
questions: Why did bad men hope the brothers would quarrel?
How did the father break the bundle?
What did the sticks stand for?
answers: So they could cheat them out of their property
He untied it and broke the sticks one at a time
The sons: together they are strong, apart they are weak
lessons.notes: An Aesop fable.

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: The Mountain Sister
steps: New words: autumn, tassels, prickly, burs, donkey
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: describe a nut-gathering day with Jeannette
If you can, find chestnuts or another nut in its shell and look inside
questions: What does the frost do for the nut gatherers?
What carries the bags of nuts?
How many nuts can be in one bur?
answers: It cracks open the prickly burs
A donkey
One to four

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: Harry and the Guidepost
steps: New words: heath, owlet, benighted, groped, dismal, betide
Read the poem aloud in a spooky voice, then a cheerful one for the ending
Narrate: what did Harry think he saw, and what was it really?
questions: What was the 'ghost'?
What did Harry decide to do the next time something frightened him?
answers: A white guidepost (signpost)
March straight up to it
lessons.notes: Poem. A guidepost is a road sign with arms pointing the way.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: The Money Amy Didn't Earn
steps: New words: tasks, season, quart, immediately, figuring
Read the lesson aloud together
Check Amy's math: 5 quarts at 13 cents, and 12 quarts at 13 cents
Copywork: “One doer is worth a hundred dreamers.”
questions: How much would Amy be paid for each quart?
How much for five quarts?
Why didn't Amy earn any money?
answers: Thirteen cents
Sixty-five cents
She spent the morning figuring, and boys picked the berries first
lessons.notes: Prices are from 1879.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: Who Made the Stars?
steps: New words: formed, brilliant, prattling, fragrant, homage, clime
Read the poem aloud; your child asks the first stanza and you answer
Memorize: the first two stanzas
questions: What question does the child ask?
Name two things the poem says God made.
answers: Who made the stars and the moon
Any two: the sun, stars, moon, leaves, flowers, feet, eyes, tongue
lessons.notes: A devotional poem written as a question and answer.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: Deeds of Kindness
steps: New words: overtook, widow, cottage, trudged, gutter, occasions
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell the two little stories of kindness
Plan one small kind deed for today
questions: Why was the woman taking apples to market?
Did the boys take apples as pay?
Why did the girl pick up the orange peel?
answers: To pay her rent
No
So no one would slip on it and fall

lessons.title: Lesson L: The Alarm Clock
steps: New words: roused, faithfully, ceased, conscience, trifling
Read the lesson aloud
Narrate: how is a conscience like the alarm clock?
questions: Why did the lady stop hearing the clock?
What is the clock compared to?
answers: She got in the habit of not obeying it
Our conscience

lessons.title: Lesson LI: Spring
steps: New words: alder, powdery, columbine, clover
Read the poem aloud, one stanza each
Memorize: the first stanza
Go outside and look for any of the plants named in the poem
questions: Name three flowers in the poem.
What sound do the frogs make?
answers: Any three: buttercups, columbine, dandelions, daisies, clover, violet
A clear, sweet music (they 'ripple')
lessons.notes: Poem by Celia Thaxter.

lessons.title: Lesson LII: True Courage
steps: New words: scholars, credit, folly, heartily, fearless
Read it as a play: assign Henry, James, and George, with you as narrator
Narrate: why does the lesson call George a coward even though he threw the snowball?
questions: Who talked George into throwing the snowball?
What would real courage have looked like?
answers: Henry
Saying no and not caring if he was laughed at
lessons.notes: Mentions whipping as a school punishment, normal in 1879. Good springboard for talking about peer pressure.

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: The Old Clock
steps: New words: steady, course, ere, wrinkled
Read the poem aloud slowly, ticking with your tongue at each “tick, tick, tick”
Copywork: “Tick, tick, tick! Time passes away.”
questions: What does Nell not understand about the clock?
Who is telling the poem?
answers: That it marks the silent passing of time
Someone older who heard the same clock as a child
lessons.notes: Poem. A short one; pair it with practice reading an analog clock.

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: The Waves
steps: New words: earnest, glorious, timid, fretful, moaning
Let your child read the lesson aloud; you read the sea's lines
Narrate: what job did each little wave do on the shore?
questions: What did the pebbles say they wanted?
Why did the big wave think he had done nothing?
What did the child on the shore notice?
answers: Washing
He only broke on a rock and splashed into a pool
The sand was clean and the water in the pool was clear

lessons.title: Lesson LV: Don't Kill the Birds
steps: New words: joyous, cheerless, warble, innocent, tuneful
Read the poem aloud together
Memorize: the first stanza
Make a list of the birds you see near your home this week
questions: What does the poem say about the life of a bird?
What would the earth be like without birds?
answers: We should not take a life we can never give
A cheerless place
lessons.notes: Poem.

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: When to Say No
steps: New words: idleness, loiter, interrupt, tempted, conceal
Read the lesson aloud, one numbered paragraph each
Narrate: list the times the lesson says to say “No”
Practice saying a polite but firm “No” to a pretend dare
questions: Why is 'No' sometimes hard to say?
What should we say when tempted to hide a wrong with a lie?
answers: Because we fear what others will think, though it is a little word
No; lying is wicked and cowardly

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: Which Loved Best?
steps: New words: pouted, rejoiced, softly
Read the poem aloud with expression
Narrate: what did John, Nell, and Fan each do after saying “I love you”?
Memorize: the last stanza
questions: Which child really loved mother best?
How did Fan show her love?
answers: Fan
She rocked the baby, swept, dusted, and helped cheerfully all day
lessons.notes: Poem by Joy Allison.

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: John Carpenter
steps: New words: satisfaction, bridle, turner, shavings, ingenious, compliment
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell how John built his horse, step by step
Make a simple toy from things around the house
questions: How much did Tom's horse cost?
Where did John get the wheels?
What did John become when he grew up?
answers: A dollar
From a turner, a man who shapes wood on a lathe
A master workman in a machine shop

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: Persevere
steps: New words: persevere, patient
Read the two stanzas aloud
Memorize: the whole poem
Copywork: “The man who travels a mile each day, / May get round the world at last.”
questions: What happens to a fisher who pulls in his net too soon?
What does 'persevere' mean?
answers: He has no fish to sell
To keep on trying and not give up
lessons.notes: Poem. Very short; pair it with review of an earlier lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson LX: The Contented Boy
steps: New words: contented, tending, errands, ninepins, obliging, Testament
Read it as a dialogue: you are Mr. Lenox, your child is Peter
Narrate: what did Mr. Lenox offer, and how did Peter answer?
questions: How did Peter help Mr. Lenox?
What did Peter do if he got hungry in the field?
What gift did Mr. Lenox promise?
answers: He caught his runaway horse
Ate a raw turnip, or went without
The books he would need for school
lessons.notes: By Dr. John Aikin (spelled Aiken in this text). An eight-year-old working in the fields was ordinary then; a dime was a lot of money.

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: Little Gustava
steps: New words: quaint, eaves, marigolds, terrier, bashful, biddy
Read the poem aloud; your child joins in on each “little Gustava” line
Narrate: list all the animals that came to Gustava's breakfast, in order
questions: What was in Gustava's bowl?
Who drank up her milk?
Which birds stayed outside?
answers: Bread and milk
Rags, the little Scotch terrier
The sparrow and the crow
lessons.notes: Poem by Celia Thaxter. 'Biddy' is an old pet name for a hen.

lessons.title: Lesson LXII: The Insolent Boy
steps: New words: insolent, abuse, dandy, skulked, tavern, injury
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns
Narrate: tell what James did to the stranger and how he found out who it was
questions: Who was the stranger?
Why had he walked into the village?
What did James lose because of his behavior?
answers: James's own uncle
To surprise his brother (James's father)
The gold watch and books his uncle had brought him

lessons.title: Lesson LXIII: We Are Seven
steps: New words: rustic, clad, porringer, kerchief, released
Read the poem aloud: you read the traveler, your child reads the little girl
Narrate: why does the girl keep saying “we are seven”?
questions: How old was the girl?
Where were two of her brothers and sisters?
What did the girl do near the graves?
answers: Eight
In the churchyard; they had died
Knitted, hemmed, sang, and ate her supper there
lessons.notes: Poem by William Wordsworth. It is about the death of two children; preview it and talk gently about loss.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV: Mary's Dime
steps: New words: sugar apples, faded, earnestly, sorrowfully, resist
Your child reads the lesson aloud as if they were Mary
Narrate: what did Mary give up, and how did she feel about it?
questions: Who gave Mary the dime?
What was Mary going to buy?
What did the beggar girl want?
answers: Her grandpa
A candy sugar apple
A gingerbread roll; she had not eaten all day

lessons.title: Lesson LXV: Mary Dow
steps: New words: innocence, delicate, forsake, rejoice
Read the poem aloud together
Narrate: tell Mary Dow's story in your own words
questions: What was Mary Dow selling?
What happened to her father?
How many matches did the speaker buy?
answers: Matches, a penny a bunch
He was lost at sea when his ship sank
All of them
lessons.notes: Poem. Children selling matches in the street was common then.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI: The Little Loaf
steps: New words: famine, eagerly, quarreled, modestly, peaceable
Read the lesson aloud
Narrate: how was Gretchen different from the other children?
questions: Why did the children quarrel?
What did Gretchen find in her small loaf?
Was the silver a mistake?
answers: Each wanted the biggest loaf
Shining silver coins
No, the baker put it there to reward her

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII: Susie and Rover
steps: New words: Newfoundland, tripped, mood, plentiful, underbrush, capered
Read the lesson together, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: what did Susie do wrong, and how did Rover show his loyalty?
questions: What did Rover carry?
Why didn't Susie enjoy the afternoon?
What did Rover do to the snake?
answers: A tin pail for the berries
She felt bad about not sharing her lunch with Rover
Seized it by the neck and killed it
lessons.notes: Adapted from Mrs. M. O. Johnson.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVIII: The Violet
steps: New words: bower, graced, humility
Read the poem aloud softly
Memorize: the first stanza
Find or draw a violet
questions: Where did the violet grow?
What does the speaker want to learn from the violet?
answers: In a green and shady bed, hidden from view
To grow in sweet humility
lessons.notes: Poem by Jane Taylor (who also wrote “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”).

lessons.title: Lesson LXIX: No Crown for Me
steps: New words: tiresome, stress, tauntingly, confessing, dignified
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns
Narrate: why did Susan throw the crown on the ground?
questions: What was Susan's task?
How did she cheat?
Did her grandmother know?
answers: Knitting twenty turns on a stocking
She moved the mark her grandmother had put in the stocking
Yes, all along

lessons.title: Lesson LXX: Young Soldiers
steps: New words: plumes, kettledrum, muskets, ramrods, gander, mullein, fray
Read the poem aloud with a marching beat
Narrate: what did the schoolboys 'fight,' and what were their weapons made of?
questions: What were the boys' muskets made of?
Which goose stood up to them?
What called them home at the end of the day?
answers: Cedar wood
One sturdy gander
The supper bell
lessons.notes: Poem about boys playing soldier. Mullein is a tall roadside weed.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI: How Willie Got Out of the Shaft
steps: New words: shaft, neighborhood, bounding, balance, sod, scampered
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: how did Willie's birthday present save him?
Talk about staying away from holes, wells, and edges
questions: What was Willie's birthday present?
Why couldn't anyone hear Willie call?
How did the letter get home?
answers: A little writing book with a pencil
He was too far from the house
Willie tied it to Caper's neck and lifted him out
lessons.notes: A shaft is a deep hole dug for a mine or well.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII: The Pert Chicken
steps: New words: pert, forward, goslings, paddling, chilled
Read the poem aloud; give the chicken a bossy voice and Mrs. Dorking a wise one
Memorize: the last stanza, “To be very wise, and show it …”
questions: Why did the chicken have so few friends?
What did he tell Mrs. Goose?
How did Mrs. Dorking put him in his place?
answers: He thought he knew everything and bossed everyone
That getting wet would kill her goslings
She reminded him he was in an eggshell a month ago
lessons.notes: Poem by Marian Douglas. A Dorking is a breed of hen.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIII: Indian Corn
steps: New words: maize, cultivated, furrows, fodder, hominy, succotash
Read the lesson aloud in two parts, stopping after paragraph 9
Narrate: how does a farmer plant 'hills' of corn, and how does the corn grow?
Look at an ear of corn: find the husk, silk, and kernels
questions: Why is it called Indian corn?
Which part of the corn plant has the male flowers?
Name three foods or products made from corn.
answers: American Indians were the first to grow it
The tassel
Any three: popcorn, hominy, succotash, cornstarch, syrup, oil, hasty pudding
lessons.notes: Uses the 1879 word 'Indians' and calls native stone bowls 'rude.' Mention that Native peoples developed corn over thousands of years.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIV: The Snowbird's Song
steps: New words: merrily, sleet, glee, frock, occasion, hobble
Read the poem aloud; your child reads the bird's answer
Narrate: what did Emily want to give the bird, and why did he say no thanks?
questions: What song did the bird sing?
What did Emily want to give the bird?
Why didn't the bird need clothes?
answers: Chick-a-de-dee
Stockings, shoes, a frock, and a hat
God had already clothed him warmly (with feathers)
lessons.notes: Poem by F. C. Woodworth.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXV: Mountains
steps: New words: ascend, retreat, rugged, torrents, chasm, precipice
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Find the Himalayas and the Andes on a map or globe
Narrate: describe a trip up the Himalayas or across an Andes pass
questions: Which mountains are the highest on earth?
What makes a bridge over a Himalayan river?
What animal carries travelers in the Andes?
answers: The Himalayas
Three ropes
The mule
lessons.notes: 'Thibet' is an old spelling of Tibet. Travel in these mountains is much easier today.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVI: A Child's Hymn
steps: New words: glow, native, comforteth, waxeth
Read the hymn aloud slowly
Memorize: one stanza of your child's choosing
Copywork: “God make my life a little light”
questions: Name the four things the child asks God to make his life like.
What does a 'little song' do in the poem?
answers: A light, a flower, a song, a hymn
Comforts the sad and helps others be strong
lessons.notes: A devotional poem.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVII: Holding the Fort
steps: New words: hobbling, sprained, lecturer, furloughs, Commandments
Read it as a dialogue: you are Genie, your child is Rob
Narrate: how did Rob sprain his ankle?
questions: What did Jack Lee do to Rob's books?
Why did Rob stop chasing Jack?
Why did Genie call Rob a 'wounded soldier'?
answers: Threw them in the mud
He remembered to return good for evil
He was hurt while doing the right thing

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVIII: The Little People
steps: New words: dreary, mirth, sterner, doleful
Read the poem aloud
Narrate: what would the world be like with no children, according to the poem?
questions: Who are the 'little people'?
What would the song of life lose without them?
answers: Children and babies
Its mirth (joy) and charm
lessons.notes: Poem by John Greenleaf Whittier.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIX: Good Night
steps: New words: hidden, watches, weary
Read the poem aloud at bedtime
Memorize: the first stanza
Celebrate finishing the Third Reader!
questions: Name three things the child says good night to.
What is lighting up the sky?
answers: Any three: father, mother, friends, birds, flowers, stars
The moon
lessons.notes: Poem by Eliza Lee Follen (Mrs. Follen). The last lesson of the book.
